div.head: Introduction
div.p: 28 August 2013. Ten people are cutting up photographs into collages at a table in the Architecture Building of Newcastle University in the UK. These images come from the Amber Film & Photography Collective’s archive of working-class life in North East England. Those taking part in the workshop titled ‘Finding new Pathways in Rich Archives’ include members of the collective, artists, and researchers [Chen et al. 2014]. They barely share a vocabulary for what an archive interface should look like. During the discussion, one participant warns that if everybody can contribute, the story they are trying to open up may be lost. However, opening the archive is the point of the exercise, but opening it too far also poses a danger to this mission. The notion of ‘opening’ carries multiple meanings. For the curator the word signals access, for the designer an interface gesture, and for the researcher a claim about interpretation. Nobody stops to fix the ambiguity of the term, and the conversation proceeds. That is what this paper is about: words that coordinate work precisely because they have not been pinned down. ‘Opening’ holds the group’s competing commitments together long enough for the more difficult negotiations to take place over what to show and on whose terms.

The workshop in Newcastle held several incompatible answers to the question of how to open an archive, let alone what an archive actually is. Archives have never been neutral repositories of evidence; from. From their inception, they have been tangled in competing projects of power, and preservation, and protection.. Born alongside the modern nation-state, historical archives both enshrined both official memory and governmental authority [Featherstone 2006]. Even in their earliest photographic manifestations, archives had a dual purpose: honorific when celebrating respected citizens, repressive when sorting bodies into criminological types [Sekula 1986]. They can be viewed as both sites of authority and sets of archiving processes that actively shape what will count as memory [Derrida 1996]. CorrespondinglyLikewise, the humanities tend to theorize the archive as a place of power and memory work, whereas archival studies aimsaim to advance more practical frameworks for creating and maintaining archives for utilitarian purposes [Caswell 2024]. A central concern of archival work is the question of provenance: , which is not merely the point of origin of archival objects, but “the network of relationships between objects, agents and functions” [Michetti 2017].2018]. Provenance is not merely the point of origin of archival objects, but the layered and evolving web of relationships in which records are embedded. Archives are approached by many with a mix of positivist promise and voyeuristic desire, drawn by the allure of recovering a lost past while attempting the “reanimation of ghostly traces” on today’s terms [Freshwater 2003].

Recent practices further expand the promise of the archive: autonomous, from activist collections mobilizemobilizing documents as tools of empowerment [Pell 2015];] to digital editors seekseeking sensory pleasure andin the flexible remediation of manuscript ecologies [Kim 2018]; and critical]. Critical archivists call for a shift from rights-based neutrality toward ‘radical empathy’empathy and liberatory memory work [Caswell &and Cifor 2016; Caswell 2021]. Against this backdrop, the digitization ofDigitizing cultural heritage positionsnow places archives at a flashpoint where: big-data surveillance and platform capitalism demand exposure and extraction at scale, while communities, curators, and scholars call for provenance, care, and epistemic justice [Bonde Thylstrup et al. 2021]. Nowhere is this tension sharper than for materials of Indigenous origin. Many cultural collections were gathered through dispossession or coercion. Now, communities are pressing fordemanding the return of these collections and for community-led governance that allows for culturally appropriate access [Russo Carroll et al. 2020]. These contradictory custodial imperatives set the stage for difficult deliberations about the design of archive interfaces.

Under pressure to widen access and empower communities while protecting sensitive materials and resisting extraction and surveillance, mixed teams consisting of digital archivists, interface designers, and humanities scholars communicate about prototypes and platforms that attempt to reconcile these conflicting demands. During such exchanges, the conversation slips into a hybrid language. Database ‘records’ mingle with discussions of ‘provenance’; ‘users’ become ‘visitors’; and the viability of a prototype is judged not primarily by ‘efficiency’ but by the likelihood of ‘serendipity’. This improvised idiom is neither the technical jargon of computer science nor the theoretical argot of cultural studies; it is a vocabulary in-between, assembled on the fly so that disparate expertise can hold a collaborative project together and pursue ambitions at the crossroads. This language offersgives teams a channel for negotiating the design implications of novel ownership or governance structures. Rather than assuming access as a given, it provides a means of deliberatingway to deliberate how and when cultural materials should be displayed or withheld, in alignment with community protocolsrather than assuming access as a given. Following the idea of disciplinary trading zones [Galison 1997], this paper recognizes this hybrid language as an emergent pidgin philosophy for the visualization of cultural collections — a contact language that enables cooperative work without perfect translation.

Visualization’s own long history foreshadows this linguistic bricolage. Long before screens or algorithms, people marked walls and knotted cords to translate experience into a compressed form — whether, from the Altamira bison drawings orto the Andean quipu cords [Urton 2017]. Such pre-historic traces remind us that various forms of knowledge representation have been braided into the longue durée of human inscriptionquipus [Drucker 2014]. ; Urton 2017]. Modernity overlaid statistical reasoning on that heritage: from William Playfair’s charts of international trade to Florence Nightingale’s diagrams of preventable death in army hospitals [Friendly and Wainer 2021]. At the beginning of the 20th century, W.E.B. Du Bois created information graphics representing African Americans’ social conditions at the turn of the 20th century [Battle-Baptiste et al.and Rusert 2018]], and a few years later Otto and Marie Neurath, along with Gerd Arntz, developed a visualization system to convey the complexity of social change in Austria [Vossoughian 2006]. Computing did not replace this lineage of visualization history but amplified and augmented it with a scientific strive for objectivity and optimization. John Tukey’s exploratory data analysis showed that algorithms could accelerate what pencils once attempted, inviting ever-larger datasets onto the screen [Tukey 1962]. Over the last two decades, projects in the digital humanities projects have re-appropriated thethese methods of data visualization, for example, to map colonial slave trade [Eltis and Richardson 2008], reveal literary correspondence networks [Edelstein et al. 2017], represent the sonic patterns of poetry [McCurdy et al. 2016], andor, more generally, provideopen up exploratory access to cultural collections [Windhager et al. 2019]. The growing use of visualization in the humanities has already prompted a reconsideration of the vocabulary for interpretative practices [Drucker 2011]. Arguably, the lexicon we adopt for visualization shapes what can be seen and what may get hidden.

What is missing is neither theory nor technique, both of which are plentiful, but a working vocabulary that survives the time frame of a particular project. This paper therefore shifts from devising new visualization techniques to doing vocabulary work: reclaiming words whose ethical articulations might keep archivalthat could keep collection interfaces open to surprise, friction, and care. It gathers three terms — wanderer, fold, and shimmer — that are starting to circulate in interdisciplinary conversations and plants them as lexical seeds that can take root in multiple soils.. Unpacking each term through feminist [D’Ignazio and Klein 2020] and pluriversal [Escobar 2018] lenses makes visible the commitments already implicit in contemporary data work and design practice. By namingNaming those commitments as part of a pidgin philosophy for data visualization, the intention is meant to embed them in the active vocabulary of interdisciplinary research and design. The terms can be understood as ‘strong concepts’ [Höök and Löwgren 2012] that can expand and express the], intermediate-level knowledge about the design of archival interfaces.

that travels between specific designs. Crucially, noticing a pidgin should not fossilize it. By: by definition, it remains open-ended, patched together from languages at hand, and remade with every new encounter [Thomason and Kaufman 1988]. Likewise, the littleThe lexicon presented here is provisional. It is offered as a kindin the spirit of a conceptual commons: a shared patch of language, open to cultivation, revision, and the planting of new lexical seeds still to come. It is important to keep the language alive and contested, for “itnot a fixed inventory. “It matters what stories make worlds, what worlds make stories” [Haraway 2016]. Vocabulary], and vocabulary work is one way to seek ways with which data visualizations can make room for many worlds at onceof remaining open for more stories than one.

In this paper, I attempt to achieve three things. First, I: 1) trace the pidgin philosophy’s emergence of the pidgin philosophy and justify vocabulary work as a methodological stance. Second, I, 2) describe three specific terms detailingthrough their lineages, theoretical commitments, and practical examples. Finally, I, and 3) synthesize these termsthem into a cross‑-cutting grammar for the design and study of archivalcollection visualizations. But before proceeding, a word on where this comes from. This is an interpretive account rather than an ethnography: in addition to readings of scholarly publications, the observations about how mixed teams talk come from co-design projects since 2013, beginning with the Newcastle workshop [Chen et al. 2014] and continuing in numerous projects in Potsdam [e.g., Dörk et al. 2020]. For this article, I coded no transcripts and counted no term frequencies. The interfaces discussed below I consider as texts to be interpreted. However, I was involved in the creation of several of them. The paper is addressed to the people who make such interfaces and to those who study them.

Following Caswell’s distinction between ‘the archive’ of humanities theory and ‘an archives’ with provenance and a custodian [Caswell 2024], I write ‘collection’ for any body of digitized cultural material and reserve ‘archive’ for cases where provenance, custodianship, or terms of access are critical. Most of the interfaces discussed in this paper are in fact museum and library projects rather than archival ones.

div.head: Pidgin Philosophy as a Living Lexicon
div.p: In historical linguistics a pidgin is a pragmatic contact language that emerges when communities without a shared language need to trade, build, or govern together [Thomason and Kaufman 1988]. Its vocabulary is blended and its grammar is minimal — just enough words and phrases to getload the ships loaded and sign the treaty signed. Conversing in pidgin means getting things done together. Arguably, pidgins. Pidgins also arise in situ between domains, exemplifying what science studies scholars may call a trading zone idiom [Galison 1997]: a stripped down but creative language that lets specialists cooperate without fully understanding one another’s disciplinary terms. Visualization projects that straddle archival studies, interface design, and digital humanities arguably show similar dynamics, when an archivist explains a finding aid convention to a visualization researcher or when a literary scholar sketches an interface idea for a designer. Fragments of archive theory, cultural studies, visual analytics, and other disciplines braidfuse into sentences that belong fully to none of the contributing fields. During co-creation workshops, design sprints, and feedback sessions, phrases like ‘serendipitous encounters’ [Foster and Ford 2003], ‘generous interfaces’ [Whitelaw 2015], ‘unfolding details’ [Bludau et al. 2020], or ‘critical cognition’ [Windhager et al. 2025] seem to appear out of nowhere, but do. They prove useful work, and, but then sometimesoften vanish once the prototypes are launched and the papers are published. The notion of ‘sandcastling’ names the ephemeral visualizations that mediate between disciplines, giving a team a word for the design process itself [Hinrichs et al. 2018]. Recognizing such fleeting speech as a pidgin helps us appreciate its performative power despite its ephemeral nature. ‘Performative’ here refers to what words can do: how language can actively shape social connections and make commitments. This emphasis on language as social action, which aligns with speech act theory and a more general performative turn in cultural studies [Bachmann-Medick 2016]. It is also evident in many Indigenous knowledge practices, where speaking is a means of establishing relations and responsibilities [Robinson 2019]. This view of language as something that acts in the world captures how certain concepts function in interdisciplinary collaborations. Considering this hybrid speech a pidgin philosophy foregrounds its pragmatic and provisional character and honors the importance of developing a shared ethos that lets collaborative work proceed before perfect translations are found...

A related concept to this pidgin philosophy is that of boundary objects, initially developed by Susan Leigh Star and James R. Griesemer in their seminal study of a natural history museum [Star and Griesemer 1989]. They found that cooperation among amateur collectors, academic biologists, and museum administrators was made possible through various objects, such as specimens, maps, and field notesmaps. These objects haditems carried different meanings for each group, yet they provided enough common structure to allow for coordinated work. In this sense, boundary objects are material or representational artifacts that bridge, bridging social worlds while accommodating divergent interests. Previous studies Boundary objects have demonstrated that boundary objects can helpsince been used to understand collaboration across institutions and worldviews. For instance, they can be utilized to study, including classification systems in queer archives [Junginger and Dörk 2021] and interdisciplinary knowledge integration [Caccamo et al. 2023]. In a similar vein, visualization artifacts produced during design study processes can themselves function as boundary objects — supporting that support sense-making and decision-making across stakeholder groups in heterogeneous organizational contexts [Otto and Davidoff 2024]. In contrast to boundary objects that center thingsartifacts, I want to foreground language itself as the medium of negotiation, focusing on terms that carry just enough resonance across disciplines to support mutual orientation. For example, ‘generosity’ and ‘serendipity’ do not function as shared artifacts, but rather as discursive bridges that help researchers deliberate values, navigate tensions, and imagine alternatives.. While boundary objects enable work despite divergent views, a pidgin philosophy can synthesize diverse perspectives into a shared vocabulary with which to develop a collective vision.

Pidgin words arecan be powerful whileduring the time frame of a project lasts, but they can evaporate once the team disbands — , forcing the next collaboration to reinvent its vocabulary from scratch. Amber is my exemplar here [Chen et al. 2014]. By the end of that afternoon a group of artists, archive members, and researchers had arrived at a shared way of describing the collection as “a living archive that grows and changes over time” and its exploration akin to “walking as an open-ended mode of engagement.” None of us could have done that in the morning. However, that shared idiom did not outlive the day. Fragments of it may have travelled on in individual speakers, but as a common language it dissolved when the group did. Rather than standardizing and preserving the language (which would diminish its agility), I would like to propose a limited lexicon as a small starting point, or rather waypoint, offor terminological reflection at the intersection of archives, design, and humanities. Debates inside humanist visualization have already revolved around naming. When Johanna Drucker argues that scholars should treat data as ‘capta’ — that is, taken, not given — she is not suggesting a new chart type but a new word to reorient research and design values [Drucker 2011]. Mitchell Whitelaw’s call for ‘generous interfaces’ likewise substitutes a moralnormative adjective for the default of efficient search, opening space for new types of interfaces that afford more exploratory encounters with in cultural collections [Whitelaw 2015]. Feminist data visualization asks designers to consider categories to be contingent, to embrace affective and embodied experiences, and to examine power relations within project teams [D’Ignazio and Klein 2016]. Across these interventions, terminology operates as a catalyst for design and critique in heterogenousheterogeneous groups. The pidgin philosophy is intended to equip interdisciplinary teams with a living lexicon to articulate what ‘good’ visualization practices might look like when aesthetics and ethics meet.

The sections that follow discuss three terms — wanderer, fold, and shimmer — that areencapsulate ideas already being exchanged in the trading zone of archivalarchive studies, interface design, and the digital humanities. Clearly, three terms do not really make a lexicon, but they serve as seeds for a grammar that synthesizes overarchingof design principles and research methods. I selected these terms because they respond to critical commitments in cultural heritage: relations over objects, duration over speed, and gaps over totality. However, someone else at this interdisciplinary crossroads would probably have picked others.

div.head: Wanderer
div.p: The figure of the wanderer offers a counterimage to the rational and rushed ‘user’ at the center of most information -seeking models. Whereas a conventional searcher may quickly scanscans a result list for relevant sources, the wanderer enters an information landscape open to gently experiencing it, willing to pause, and ready to be surprised. In doing so, the wanderer engages with archives with attentiveness and empathy. This disposition fosters a kind of care — for overlooked materials, for the invisible labor of collection-making, and for the stories that connect different archival worlds.

div.head: Origins
div.p: The notion of a calm and curious wanderer originates in the nineteenth -century flâneur strolling the streets of Paris [Baudelaire 1965] [; Benjamin 1973], but should be broadened here to include wayfarers [Ingold 2007] and the flaneuse [Elkin 20162017]. Prior work draws from the historical figure of the flâneur to formulate design cues for digital interfaces: just as the urban stroller drifts between arcades and alleyways, an information flaneur moves from item to item, noticing beauty, tension, and contradiction along the way [Dörk et al. 2011]. Echoing the qualities of exploratory search [Marchionini 2006] and leisurely browsing [Morse et al. 2021], the information flaneur engages in open-ended and casual information seeking. This poetic persona is a deliberate rejection of deficiencybaseddeficiency-based conceptions of information seekers. It replaces, replacing the anxious searcher with a curious, critical, and creativean attentive wanderer [Dörk et al. 2011].

While the digital environments may appear disembodied, the politics of movement still apply — shapingshape who feels entitled, safe, or and welcome to explore at leisure. The flâneur’s freedom to look and linger depended on a range of social and economic privileges. Susan Buck-Morss complicates idealized notions of the flâneur and places him on a continuum with the street’s less celebrated, more marginalized figures [Buck-Morss 1986]. In her reading, flânerie is possible only within a political economy that turns idleness into both commodity and threat; the. The gaze that lingers in front of shop windows is never far from the policing of loitering. Feminist thinkers show how women’s movement throughElizabeth Wilson presses the question further, arguing that the flâneur is less a figure of mastery than of unease, and that the city has been threatened by harassment for women both a site of danger and one of unexpected freedom [Wilson 1992]. Critical race scholars further demonstrate how a Even so, the freedom to linger has never been evenly distributed. Simone Browne shows how racialized surveillance system considersrenders unhurried movement suspect, while the same slowness is read as suspicious loitering unlessleisure when practiced by white pedestrians, which is then celebrated as leisurely wandering [Browne 2015]. These dynamics carry over to digital space, where freedom to wander is increasingly constrained by bandwidth, language, censorship, and tracking systems. Digital analogies of the leisurely stroll must confront the politics of who gets to wander where and under which conditions. In addition, wanderingWandering in an archive unfolds both within and in tension with its rules of gathering and organizing contents and the terms of entry [Derrida 1996]. Rather than claiming frictionless access, wanderer-aware interfaces could make thresholds legible — : who is hosted, under what authority, and which traces are retained.

To challenge the androcentric and Eurocentric pedigree of the flaneur, we braid two complementary threads can be woven into the wanderer. First, feminist flânerie foregrounds safety, self-definition, and resistance against surveillance [Elkin 2017]. ArchivalCollection interfaces should expose positionality cues and allow annotation layers where marginalized wanderers can leave counternarratives. Second, Indigenous wayfaring reframes movement as relation-making [Ingold 2007]. Building on Inuit conceptions of travel, characterize wayfaring is seen as a way of being, in which the traveler quite literally becomes the line of travel, sustaining identity through an unfolding mesh of paths that link people, animals, and land as co-participants rather than as origins and destinations. A wanderer-aware interface can echo this by visualizing relational aspects of collections — e.g., showmaking relations visible: how a photograph is tied to land, kin, or species — , and by letting users followwhere those threads lead if followed laterally rather than drilling down hierarchically.a hierarchy. Together these perspectives shift wandering from idle luxury to an ethic of attentive movement: slowly traversing digital environments slowly enough to perceive what is usually overlooked and to become receptive to the entanglements that shape our position in time and space.

div.head: Meanings
div.p: To embrace the ethos of the wanderer during design, archival navigationnavigating the collection as a kind of wandering can be translated into three commitments for digital interfaces.

Mindful meandering. Interfaces that serve wanderers should let curiosity, not efficiency, dictate movement. Instead of channeling visitors through a search box toward a ranked list, a wander-aware design offers multiple thresholds — random items, semantic maps, thematic trails — and represents progress as a branching constellation rather than a breadcrumb line. Visual cues can hint at untaken side streets, encouraging the wanderer to drift laterally and discover the archive’scollection’s breadth before diving into depth. In some ways, thisThis resembles the common experience in a physical reading room, where the careful handling of boxes and files often leads to slow, attentive discovery. Yet in digital settings, slow looking often registers as inactivity in analytics dashboards, even though it is central to the ethos of wandering. The importance of slowness is also echoed in Indigenous pedagogies, where slow reflection is essential to learning and being in the world [Leddy and Miller 2020]. Designers can affirm the value of slow perusal by disabling aggressive session time-outs, preserving navigation histories, and displaying subtle hints that affirmaffirming that browsing without hurry is welcome. Such cues reassure visitors that thoughtful hesitation is not only permitted but encouraged, fostering deeper engagement with complex materials.

Relational revelation. A wanderer’s detours are most rewarding when they expose hidden ties. Whenever an item comes into view, the interface should foreground its web of relationships — among linked people, places, events, materials, and subjects — through expandable halos, contextual sidebars, or pivot buttons that invite lateral hops.. By letting wanderers move across these relational views, the interface honors the archive’scollection’s layered structure and helps visitors sense how any single record participates in larger, intertwined stories. This vision aligns with long-standing efforts in the heritage community to model complex connections among records, actors, and contexts. Notably, Records in Contexts (RiC) by the International Council on Archives provides a framework for representing records in a graph of of entities and relations via creators, subjects, places, and datesfor archival description [ICA 2023]. Similarly, CIDOC-CRM provides a general ontology for expressing event- and object-based connections across archives, libraries, and museums [ICOM 20252024]. When a visualization exposes these links, metadata ceases to be back-room matter and becomes the very substancepart of exploratory travel.

Reflexive gaze. Looking is never neutral; who. Who we are shapes what we see, and archives are thick with symbols of power. Interfaces cancould surface this situatedness — and invite critique — through lightweight changes to wording to let, letting wanderers reflect on their own position in relation to the archive. Role badges such as ‘public passerby,’ ‘contributing member,’ or ‘registered researcher’ cancould appear in the header and could be toggled or dismissed, reminding every wanderer that the view is partial and shaped by standpoint. Such framing could would ideally be developed in collaboration with the communities whose materials are held, so that the roles reflect lived relationships to the archive. At the same time, infrastructuralInfrastructural aspects — such as scanner settings, digitization credits, and redaction notices — might hover at the margins, pointing to the labor, privilege, or censorship beneath each record. A clicktrailFurthermore, a clickstream layer letscould let visitors inspect their own paths, asking whether they have drifted into confirmation loops or entered unfamiliar ground. These commitments shift the design question from “How do we guide users to items quickly?” to “How do we host wanderers so they can linger, wonder, and connect within and across archival worlds?”

Because wandering privileges open-ended movement, it can clash with institutional requirements for preservation, copyright, or cultural protocol. Designers must therefore negotiate between openness and sovereignty. For Indigenous archives, wanderer -centered interfaces should default to invitation-based rather than unrestricted download;. In addition, for sensitive community collections, wandering maycould be staged through curated pathways coauthored with stakeholders. Accessibility is another stake: exploratory navigation must be viable via screen reader and on low -bandwidth connections. Providing alternative text for visual material and offering lightweight webpages can help make sure that wandering is not reserved for the fully sighted or broadband -privileged.

div.head: Usage
div.p: With these commitments in hand, we can turn from the abstract to the concrete. The ethos of the wanderer is already partially realized by tangible features andin interaction patterns intechniques of experimental collection interfaces. TheIn the following, three examples demonstrate the practical viability of wandering as an alternative mode of access and appreciation.

Collections Dive
Collections Dive was created for Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums as a probe into tempo-based browsing [Coburn 2016]. Visitors enter a generous grid of thumbnail tiles that stretches far beyond the viewport and is replenished continuously when scrolling down. The engine samples the aggregated corpus according to scroll speed: a leisurely glideslow scrolling returns objects with similar metadata with those already in view, whereas a rapid swipeobjects, fast scrolling retrieves artifacts from distant curatorial domains. Crucially, everyEvery click shows more details ofdetail on a given item. By couplingCoupling tempo-sensitive drift andwith a reflective navigation network, this playful interfaceinteraction demonstrates how an archive a collection interface could cultivate attentiveness, surface latent relationships without hierarchy, and reveal one’s path to invite reflection about what was chosenon the path that led there.

Dive into Color [Vane 2019] takes a different route, using perceptual hue as the organizing logic for artifacts drawn from Cooper Hewitt’s design holdings. After selecting a segment in a color wheel, matching catalog records are rendered as tiles placed along a temporal layout. Because hue rarely maps neatly onto curatorial taxonomies, browsing becomes an act of lateral association: a vase with blue décor may nudge up against a blue soup spoon. Curators testing the interface report that the layout can trigger questions calling attention toabout gaps in metadata, as when a certain hue selection generates an oddly sparse timeline. A side drawer tracks every tile the viewer hovers over, allowing that chromatic detours canto be taken. In concert, theretraced. Later items appear above the selection and earlier ones below, so that scrolling up or down moves forward or backward in time [Bludau et al. 2021].

Where the previous two projects privilege an open drift, the Relational Perspectives interface for the Raoul Hausmann collection invites visitors to pivot the corpus from successive item-based vantage points [Bludau et al. 2021]. The entry mosaic presents a flattenedfaceted overview, but once an artifact is chosen, threeit is placed in the middle of the interface in the context panels — material attributes, content keywords, and temporal chronology — become active in the same frame.of related items (see Figure 1). Each click on another artifact re-centers the display on the new focal item, enabling lateral hops among photographs, collages, and letters without losing orientation. In practice this produces, producing an almost kaleidoscopic form of navigation. The temporal view makes indeterminacies more explicit — , with gradient bands stretchstretching across spans where dates are ambiguous — thereby, surfacing the gaps in collection knowledge.

Against the three commitments these examples are uneven. All three interfaces support mindful meandering, and two support relational revelation (Collections Dive and Relational Perspectives). Reflexive gaze is absent from all three, since none tells a visitor who they are taken to be or what is being logged about them. Wandering as movement is well developed. However, wandering as a situated and observed act is not (yet) well supported.

div.head: Fold
div.p: Having followed the wanderer along the archive’s shelves and boxes, we now consider the fabric of those structures themselves. If the wanderer foregrounds attentive movement, the fold orients us to the form of the interface: the mutable contours that appear, and contract, and reappear as we drag, scroll, and click. Just as a traveler rolls and unrolls a map to reveal new routes without tearing the paper, a folding interface must expand detail while preserving the context of the whole. We now trace this idea from its philosophical origins to the practical manifestations of folds in archival interfaces.

div.head: Origins
div.p: The fold enters contemporary theory through Gilles Deleuze’s reading of Leibniz, where every phenomenon is figured as a pleated surface whose successive explications, implications, and complications knit thought to matter [Deleuze 1993]. In visualization research the metaphor has been adopted to describe zooms, semantic lenses, and other interactions that reveal fine detail without disrupting the larger context [Brüggemann et al. 2020]. Deleuze’s baroque lineage, however, is only one thread. Across many Indigenous traditions, folding and weaving operate not as metaphors but as world-making practices that bind entities into durable relations.

Many Indigenous knowledge systems understand folding and weaving not as metaphors but as ontological practices that make the world. In Mesoamerica, the very topology of the cosmos is conceived as a fabric whose solar obverse and intensive reverse are articulatedseparated, and so brought into being, by an incessant operation of folding — , the act that allows spirits to surface in human time and persons to dissolvemovement by which fragments of the other side fold themselves into the solar world and solar beings unfold back into the virtual domain [Pitarch 2021]. Textile arts supply the conceptual template for this cosmology: ritual bundles, and body wrappings, and even speech itself are understood as folds that momentarily stabilize a heterogeneous multiplicity before it slips away again. Here, to fold is already to relate;, and every crease is an event of passage and transformation. A comparable logic is articulated in Australian Aboriginal philosophies of twining and plaiting. Warlpiri elders describeand Yolŋu thought. In dialogue with Samuel Curkpatrick, the senior Warlpiri elder and scholar Wanta Jampijinpa Pawu describes ngurra-kurlu (home-having) as a cosmicpattern for living handed down from the ancestors, one that shows how everything is related. It has many names, one of them sacred and spoken only by men in initiation ceremony. That name has to do with weaving and is also a name for the Southern Cross, whose stars weave in which people and places are physically connected by fibers; to live well is to be woven by the land, drawing distinct strands together without erasing their integrityinto the diamond shape representing the whole of ngurra-kurlu. As Pawu puts it, it is not you who does the weaving: country weaves you, so that you become your ngurra (home) [Curkpatrick et al. 2023]. The Southern Cross figures as interlaced star threads celebrated in the form of the Among Yolŋu, raki’ (string) that joins kin across time and space. The strength of the weave lies in), twined from the bark fiber of the kurrajong tree in Wägilak ceremonial song from northeast Arnhem Land, stands for the connection between a present generation and its tension: surfaces remain taut because unseen strandsancestors, and for the obligations and attachments that hold them from beneath.kin to one another [Curkpatrick et al. 2023].

A further dimension of the fold emerges in Indigenous critiques of colonial archives, where it can also mark sites of erasure, concealment, and woundedness. As Dana Claxton articulated at the Crossing Fonds symposium [Claxton 2024], Indigenous knowledge often enters the archive not by invitation, but through appropriation — , and the fold becomes a space where such knowledge is withheld in shadow. In her view, the fold carries the wounds of the archive, holding the dual potential for harm as well as for healing. Rather than a neutral affordance, the fold becomes a site of continual refolding. Claxton’s vision complicates the aesthetics of inclusion by asking whether the archive’s folds can ever be complete without Indigenous presence — , or whether they must remain in tension, stitched but never sealed.

Recognizing these varied genealogies reframes the fold from an elegant philosophical trope into a situated, relational ethic. Data never arrive as neutral sheets waiting to be pleated;. Instead, power, custodianship, and vulnerability are already woven through them. A folding interface that expands an archive record while keeping provenance visible, or that leaves restricted materials enveloped unless proper ceremony is observed, honors this ethic.

div.head: Meanings
div.p: When weaving aspects of the fold into visual interfaces, four intertwined qualities can guide the design process: coherence, elasticity, infinity [Brüggemann et al. 2020], and depth.

Coherence requires that every partial view remains visibly tethered to the broader weave. Collapsing a family branch, filtering by period, or zooming out must leave the overall framework intact so that relations stay legible even when compressed. A foldingcollection interface must thereforeshould let readers open a facet of an archive without severing it from the fabric it rests on. A fold that erases its hidden layers, like a mat whose edge unravels, breaks trust with both data and viewer.

Elasticity values supple transformation over brittle jumps. Interactive sliders, drag-to-weight controls, or touch-based stretch gestures should let the visual fabric give and rebound as interests evolve, signaling that knowledge is dynamic yet continuous.. Micro-animations that show nodes elongating before they settle or timelines bending under pressure materialize this ethical softness: they announce make a change of view legible. Elasticity is a claim about interfaces, not on knowledge. Collections are full of discontinuities, in the form of destroyed, stolen, or withheld records. Applied indiscriminately, elasticity can smooth those gaps into a gradient. While a break that is an artifact of the current view can be animated, a break that no inquirybelongs to the collection should tear the strands holding records togetherstand out.

Infinity acknowledges that every unfolding is provisional. The word needs qualifying, since collections are indeed finite. What is open is the set of relations, not the holdings. Gradient fades at the canvas edge, captions that read ‘further relations continue beyond this zoom,’ oror the refusal to display a triumphant ‘all items loaded’ badge, remind visitors that deeper pleats remain out of sight — , sometimes because of cultural protocol, sometimes because the archivecollection is simply unfinished. Infinity, here, is Better than a soft edge is a named one: this holding ends in this year because the donor’s papers do, or two hundred items are restricted and appear in no view. Stated that way, the exposed finitude is provenance information rather than a defect to be visually softened, while infinity conveys an ethic of humility: a fold is never final, and the interface design should keep the horizon of yet-unseen stories open.

Depth frames the fold as a layered space of memory. Every fold introduces a surface, but also a recess — , something set aside, hidden, or held in reserve. This depth is not simply a matter of scale, but of responsibility: what lies beneath may be sacred, or wounded, or uncertain.. Designing with depth means acknowledging that not everything in an archivea collection should be immediately seen. It allows, allowing space for latency, and partiality, and silence.. Visually, this can be signaled by shadow, blur, or layering — elements that hint without fully revealing.. Depth unfolds in time, through gestures that require pause, resistance, or reciprocal engagement before proceeding.

In short, the The fold offers a productive counterproposal to flattened dashboards, static visualizations, and rigid result lists. Rather than pretending that data display is friction-free, it treats interaction as the skilled weaving and handling of cloth: stretching to reveal, relaxing to protect, and always acknowledging the fibers that must not be tugged. Seen through this lens, each view change is also a moment of disclosure. Does a faceted filter sever a record from its custodial kin, or does it leave a visible selvedge of context? Does an animated transition merely entertain, or does it let the visitor feel the tension that holds heterogeneous strands together? Akin to the idea of seamful visualizations exposing the stitches of their own making and the contingencies of the underlying data [Hengesbach 2022], a folding interface earns trust not by hiding imperfections but by letting viewers sense where the weave is patched, provisional, or worn thin. Designing with folds, then, is designing with seams: respecting archival thickness, rendering its threads and knots perceptible, and inviting users to judge for themselves where the fabric can safely be further un-folded and where it ought to remain gathered or worn thin.

div.head: Usage
div.p: The practical reach of folding has already been mapped in visualization research. A recent survey on un/foldable data visualizations [Bludau et al. 2025] catalogs more than a hundred techniques that rely on progressive revealing and compressing rather than window-switching or pop-up layering. Across widely different data domains the survey demonstrates the same guiding logic: new detail is woven into the graphic surface, while contextual cues remain present whileas scale shifts, and interaction is rendered fluid enough for the eye to bridge successive states. The review shows that folds. Folds are neithernot rare novelties nor discipline-specific techniques; they formbut an emerging design pattern for visualizations of complex, stratified information. To see how this concept can be expressed in the context of digital collections, we now considerIn the following, three visualcollection interfaces each of which implementillustrate the idea of folds in a distinct mannerways.

Figure 2: Past Visions with the drawings filtered by the keyword Potsdam. Images that do not match fade and settle below the timeline, so the filtered selection stays legible against the whole collection rather than replacing it [Glinka et al. 2017].

Past Visions [Glinka et al. 2017] is a dynamic visualization environment accommodating 1,492 nineteenth-century drawings by Frederick William IV of Prussia (1795-1861) on a zoomable and filterable canvas. [Glinka et al. 2017]. The landing view positions every sheet — pertaining to a broad range of topics from urban planning to poetry — as a tiny thumbnail along a timeline whose granularity grows or shrinks as the viewer zooms into or out of the arrangement. The timeline features historical and biographical information contextualizing this collection. At the top of the interface is a linearized word cloud featuring subjects and themes characterizing the drawings. Filtering by theme gradually reshapes the arrangement of tags and images. The thumbnails not matching any selection criteria become translucent and gently move below the timeline. (see Figure 2). Every state change is animated in place;. In contrast to conventional interfaces, nothing jumps to a new window. At the maximum magnification the resolution is so high that it is possible to see the texture of pencil strokes and paper grain. Anonymous usage logs suggest that the gradually zoomable environment invites a rhythm of approach and retreat rather than a one-way drill-down.

From zooming to scrolling, Reading Traces visualizes Theodor Fontane’s (1819-1898) hand-library in a flexible form that can be gradually expanded and compressed via continuous scroll movements [Bludau et al. 2020]. The interface opens on a shelf-like band of 155 vertical bars, each bar a book; the varying widths of the bars encode how densely Fontane annotated that volume. Scrolling downward echoes running a finger along the spines: bars lengthen into page strips, and, with a further scroll, individual marginalia come out as colored squares that give access to facsimile scans. Scrolling in the opposite direction, the individual bars eventually merge into an overview summarizing the traces for each author. Every reveal occurs in place. When the viewer shifts between different granularities, the bars and curves gradually shift — stretching, compressing, but neverstretch and compress without ever disappearing — , allowing the eye to track continuity across different scales. Resembling a complication in Deleuze’s terms, a toggle in the sidebar pivots the display into a similarity arrangement that is based on the character and frequency of marginalia left by Fontane for each author or book.

A different folding tactic guides Close-up Cloud [Junginger et al. 2020],, a visualization prototype built around the glass negatives by the photographer Wilhelm Weimar (1857-1917) at Hamburg’s Museum for Art and Design. [Junginger et al. 2020]. Instead of presenting a synoptic overview first, as in the other cases, the interface begins as a graphical tag cloud featuring cropped details — such as leaf ornaments and embroidered letters — whose tile size reflects how often that motif occurs in the corpus. The tiles transition with a gentle cross-fading animation between different instances of the tag across the collection. Hovering over any tile reveals the tag’s name and frequency; clicking recenters. Clicking on a tile centers the view and unfolds all the close-ups that sharesharing this tag grouped by the respective glass negatives on which this tag has been placed. A second click on an item’s tile gently moves all the close-ups belonging to this negative to their exact coordinates on the original image, after which the full plate fades in, only then completing a cohesive and completefull image of a glass negative. Visitors can flip the entire display from negative to positive, converting the abstract originals into their more intuitive counterparts that better convey depth of the depicted artworks and design objects. The smooth transitions — from the fragmented view of details in the visual tag clouddetail views to the cohesive overview of a single object — views illustrate how folding can invert the usual hierarchy of overview and detail: viewers begin immersed in minute fragments and only later assemble a coherent artifact, seeing the collection gradually unfold around the paths they take in the interface.

Coherence and elasticity are where these three are relatively strong, and depth is partly there: each stages the collection in layers and requires a descent to reach any single item. Its other half, the refusal to show, is untested since none of these collections holds restricted material. Infinity fares worst: a bounded, fully digitized corpus in each case, with no signal of what is missing.

div.head: Shimmer
div.p: ArchivalCollection interfaces are more than just scaffolds and surfaces. They can be filled withhold moments that feel alive, beckoning usthe visitor to pause and take alook closer look. These brief,. Such radiant moments are what can be called shimmer: a pulse of relational brilliance that illuminatesdiscloses a hidden connectionsconnection and reminds ussuggests that every archivea collection is a living ecology, not rather than a static repository. Shimmer is playful and unpredictable. The concept of shimmer can breathe new life into archival data visualization. Of, and of the three terms discussed in this paper, this oneit is perhaps the most speculative when it comes to the design of archival interfacescollection visualizations.

div.head: Origins
div.p: The English word ‘shimmer’ suggestsrefers to a wavering gleam, yet the concept is given far greater depth in the Yolŋu languages of northern Australia. There, bir’yun refers tonames the moment whenbrilliance a surface — such as bark, skin, a leaf, or water — transitions acquires once it has been worked from dull to brilliant and begins to vibrate withbright, a shimmer in which ancestral presencepower is felt to be present [Morphy 1989]. Just as a sudden break in a cloud can cause a river to flash, the finely cross-hatched lines of a painting can emit a similar radiance. Deborah Bird Rose extends this concept to include multispecies lures: blossoms attractthe blossom that attracts flying-fox pollinators, songlines draw dancers into ceremonies,the patterns of song and dance that light up a ceremony, or the gleam of sunlight glints on wet stone to draw human attentionleaves [Rose 2022]. In this sense, shimmerShimmer is nevertherefore not a static property. Rather, it is an event of reciprocal held by any one thing but a capture — a moment running in which divergent beings seize one anotherseveral directions at once: water reflecting the sun, the sun glinting on the water, the eyes of the beholders caught and experience shared vitality. Thisheld. However, that vitality is precarious. Like many vibrant things on a damaged planet, it is at risk of fading away. Rose writes that “extinction cascades drag shimmer from the world” as relationships falter and species disappear [Rose 2017]. The concept therefore carries a built-in ethics: toTo notice shimmer is to sense both beauty and peril, animation and its potential loss.. When shimmerthe term migrates into digital interfaces, we must bring the baggage comes with us.it. While the effect itself travels across cultures, its interpretation does not. A graphic that sparkles for mere effect dilutes the term; a pulseresembles the stimulus, but drops everything that marks living, threatened ties honors its lineagemade it mean anything.

div.head: Meanings
div.p: Shimmer belongs to the family of what anthropologist Anna Tsing calls ‘arts of noticing’ [Tsing 2015]:: practices that train perception to catch short-lived signals of entanglement before they slip away. [Tsing 2015]. In Yolŋu thought, bir’yun materializes only atis a quality of the instant whenworked surface, light, and viewer align;a painting need not even be seen for that quality to do its work: most ritual paintings are covered or rubbed out within hours, and much of the experience of them is a glimpse from the corner of the eye. The brilliance is therefore relational and contingent rather than intrinsic or deterministic. Three complementary meanings emerge from this termin its meaning, which is culture-specific, while the experience of being captured by it reaches across cultures.

Ephemeral encounter. Translating shimmer to archivalcollection visualization demands that we reconceive graphical accent not as ornament but as a momentary co-presence between archival aggregationsthe aggregated collection and the wandering visitor. Because shimmer is inherently fleeting, it gestures toward a temporal ethics. It does not promise continuous access; instead, it models a shift in its appearance that respects ceremonial timing, ecological cycles, or community protocols. In design terms, this may mean valuing latency and recurrence over permanence, making room for absence as an integral part of presence.

Precarious allure. Shimmer also carries the experience of fascination towards an entity that is at risk of destruction. The flash of vitality can slide into voyeuristic spectacle if severed from context, yet declining to lure at all risks rendering fragile ties invisible. The conceptual challenge is to hold allure in tension with responsibility: illumination must come twinned with an offer to reciprocate — , through credit, or stewardship, or a commitment to protect.

Partial survival. Finally, shimmer invites an ontology of loss and incompleteness. The warning that extinction pulls shimmer from the world suggests that visualization should not cling to wholeness but acknowledge attrition. The interface becomes a site where viewers confront what is missing or fading, and where brilliance itself is recognized as an index of vulnerability. Under this ethic, shimmer is not only an aesthetic flourish but an alarm, calling attention to relations that need care if they are to keep glimmeringincompleteness. Brilliance indicates vitality, while its withdrawal registers loss. Rose distinguishes between dullness as a phase in a pulse, a resting state that can brighten again, and dullness as a flat absence. An interface that dims can mean either, and telling the two apart is the design problem: a collection between states looks much like one that is disappearing. A greyed-out facet may indicate a record under embargo, a digitization backlog, or a holding that no longer exists, and only the first of these will return. Shimmer therefore works as an invitation, calling attention to relations that need care if they are to persist.

These three strands suggest that shimmerShimmer in an archivea collection interface should therefore not be decorative sparkle but a carefully staged moment of lively, risky presence: it appears only long enough to createallow a charge of curiosity and accountability, then dims so that other relations can come forward. Whether shimmer can be designed at all is doubtful. The effect is the tractable part, since brilliance is produced by technique and the light in a cross-hatched painting is real. What cannot be arranged is what a viewer brings to it, and it is there that the meaning of bir’yun stays with the source communities. A designer can only prepare conditions. This makes shimmer a term of reflection and interpretation more than of implementation or evaluation.

What these three interfaces share is an openness to something that cannot be ensured. Any brilliance in them arrives, if it arrives at all, from a particular viewer meeting a unique arrangement in a specific situation. This makes shimmer the weakest of the three terms as a specification for design, yet a clear illustration of what vocabulary work can do. A concept that can neither be implemented nor measured still has the capacity to change what a diverse team may decide to leave room for.

div.head: A Grammar for Visual ArchiveCollection Interfaces
div.p: At this point, the three terms are discrete entries in a small dictionary. However, anyA pidgin becomes only useful only when words form phrases in acts of speech. The terms gain real force when they are spoken in the situations where interfaces are imagined, created, and evaluated: from interpreted: co-design workshops and, community reviews to, field deployments, and studio pedagogy. What follows is an attempt to outlineoutlines a grammar for visual archivecollection interfaces. First, theThe principles formulate overarching commitments. Next, a phrase book showssuggests how the terms can be combined in various settings. Finally, a , and a research framework binds the pidgin philosophy to a transdisciplinaryproposes a methodology.

div.head: Principles
div.p: The three lexical seeds — wandererWanderer, fold, and shimmer — share more than a convenient rhetorical affinity. Together they formsuggest a miniature theorycoherent way of thinking about interface design for archival datacollection visualizations grounded in the importance of connections, timing, and gaps.

Relationality. Conventional information systems treat data as self-contained objects waiting to be retrieved. By contrast, the proposedThe pidgin philosophy redirects attention to the ties that bind entities together and to the actors who forge and traverse those ties. The wanderer, for instance, is defined not by arrival at a target but by a continuously renegotiated distance between self, record, and contexts. The archiveA collection is not a closed trove but a space for responsive accumulation: wanderers may annotate, trace paths, or offer commentary, not as external observers, but as participants in an expanding web of relations. rather than as external observers. A fold does not add more content; it, but reorganizes adjacency, bending and bends layers so thatto center peripheral items can come to the center.. Shimmer makesputs the relational focus unmistakable:most sharply. The brilliance occurs only inis produced by the surface, but what it comes to mean depends on what the split-second when two entities meet — viewer and record, human and more-than-humanbrings to the encounter. While it may seem romantic, shimmer points to a moment of affective tension in a situated encounter. In an archivala collection interface built on the principle of relationality, the default unit of design is a connection (: a co-citation, a shared provenance tag, or a kinship line), and the success of a session is measured less by items accessed than by the relations perceived and pursued.

Temporality. Standard usability doctrine values immediacy — : pages that load in under two hundred milliseconds, search results that stream as you type. The pidgin philosophy argues instead for animations, transitions, and intermissions that give temporal texture to the archivecollection interface. The wanderer’s slow drift encourages hesitation and side-tracking;, while the folds stretch or compress the movement between overview and detail, letting the eye acclimate; shimmer. Shimmer offers an evanescent pulse that may or may not recur, reminding viewers that archivescollections, like ecosystems, breathe. Designing with multiple tempos entails choreographing moments of stillness (, such as a lingering hover before metadata blooms) and, alongside bursts of intensity (a sudden flash that flags endangered lineage). The orchestration of. Attention to tempo counters the flattening effect of real-time dashboards and rapid responses, returning duration and rhythm to inquiry.

Partiality. The seedsthree terms also converge on an ethics of necessary incompleteness. Wandering accepts that some corridors remain closed; folds keep certain pleats latent to honor custodianship or cognitive load; shimmer appears only when conditions are right. Friction and refusal, often treated as obstacles to be engineered away, could become design affordances in their own right. This stance resonates with feminist critiques of full disclosure as a colonial gesture, Indigenous data-sovereignty protocols [Russo Carroll et al. 2020], and growing privacy concerns [Windon and Youngblood 2024]. While archival policies increasingly accommodate such ethics, interface design has yet to catch up: few systems make partiality perceptible as part of the uservisitor experience. Interfaces that embrace partiality should therefore build in graceful dead-ends, consent-to-unfold gates, and quiet indicators that something is withheld. They teach visitors that not-knowing can coexist productively with open exploration.

Relationality, temporality, and partiality offer a compact but robust set of general principles for archivalcollection visualizations that foreground ties over nodes, rhythm over speed, and care over completeness.

div.head: Research framework
div.p: Because the grammar of the pidgin philosophy claims equal fidelity to design practice, as much as to interpretive scholarship, and empirical rigor, its research program should braidcombine methods drawn from those distinct traditions. We I organize the braidthem into three overlapping passes that can repeat and inform each other in any order: designerly probing, humanistic reading, and technicalsituated evaluation.

Designerly probing treats the prototypevisualization creation as a research instrumentprocess in its own right. Here the team works through iterative sandcastles [Hinrichs et al. 2018] that materializefollow one heuristicemerging question at a time: a constellation view that foregrounds wandering;, or an elastic stack that resembles folding; a low-contrast pulse that experiments with shimmer.. Situated cultural-probe exercises — , such as sketchbooks, sound-maps, or speculative postcards — , can prompt participants to voice sensory memories and contested readings of a place, demonstrating how in-situ design probes stimulate plural, critical perspectives on cultural heritage [Schofield et al. 2019]. Collaborative critique sessions borrow from reflective practice: to inform iterations, collages are pinned up and openly discussed in the group to inform the next iteration [Dörk et al. 2020]. The outcome is not a finished product but a clarified design question, carried forward as a hypothesis.

Humanistic reading enters next. Prototypereplays prototype sessions are replayed as if they were texts: screen recordings and transcriptions of think-aloud expressions become trace documents for close reading and thick description. Researchers annotate the momentRather than asking whether a hover turns intovisitor completed a shimmer or stagetask, the reading asks what a slow walk throughpause was doing, where an expectation was disappointed, and which vocabulary a corpusparticipant reached for when the interface offered none. Collaborators should pursue their own readings of prototypes to expose latent power relations. Community partners add situated critique — formulate ‘friendly critique’ and give suggestions for iterations. Indigenous elders may refuse a fold that exposes restricted knowledge or, while poets may celebrate a wandering path that produces serendipitous juxtapositions. These hermeneutic moves return ethical and cultural nuance to what could otherwise could remain purely interactional data.

Empirical evaluation closes the loop without closing down inquiry. Instrumented prototypes log quantitative traces that correspond to specific terms. Statistical models then test whether a revised fold improves orientation or whether a gentle animation increases lateral hops without shortening total dwell time. When machine-learning components guide adaptive shimmer or recommend new folds, the same logs are audited for algorithmic bias: does guidance nudge visitors toward a particular community’s materials at the expense of others?

Situated evaluation investigates how the pidgin philosophy holds up in real encounters with an interface. However, the canonical metrics tend to capture the wrong thing. Dwell time, click depth, and task completion may measure efficiency, but a wanderer who lingers is indistinguishable from a visitor who has left the room. Logs can be useful, but as traces to be read rather than aggregated. A single session replayed as a path shows where a visitor doubled back, which unfolding was abandoned midway, and when a threshold was never crossed. In addition to these, observations and interviews with visitors, curators, archivists, and community members can determine if the terms represent anything meaningful in their encounters with the collection.

The three passes circulate in a spiral. Quantitative anomalies — say, a drop in continuity — A puzzling pattern in the traces may send designers back to build another prototype; hermeneutic insight — perhaps a poetic, while a close reading of a shimmer fade — fold that participants consistently misread suggests alternative metrics such as interpretive resonance; and designa different kind of vocabulary. Design iterations produce new datamaterial for computational testsinterpretation. Throughout, the open glossary serves as a running ledgerkind of knowledge base: heuristics are tagged with empirical notes, metrics observations, terms fork into stricter or looser dialects, and new termswords enter the vocabulary when existing ones no longer capturespeak to an emerging practice.

Balancing designerly, humanistic, and technological inquiry in this way does more than triangulate validity; it enacts the pidgin philosophy in a mixed method. Each strand honors relationality (through collaboration across expertise),, temporality (through an iterative rhythm rather than a waterfall),, and partiality (through the admission that no single method or measure can claim total truth), ensuring that the research framework remains as plural and reflexive as the grammar it seeks to refine.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: This pidgin philosophy sets out a vocabulary and grammar for the design and study of data visualizations of archival fonds and cultural collections, yet several important aspects fall outside the scope of this paper. Below I briefly acknowledge key concerns that are readable as shortcomings of the framework or as directions for future work.

Infrastructural debt. Behind every elegant interface lies a hidden accrual of technical and organizational liabilities. Digitization backlogs often delay whole swaths of a collection;, while grant cycles dictate which servers are patchedmaintained and which silently age; cold. Cold-storage cloud tiers can make a master file effectively unreachable just when a community demands higher-resolution evidence. As the Endings Project has shown, most cultural‐-heritage sites are launched with short-term funds but without a plan — or the institutional labor — to migrate code, refresh formats, or document bespoke stacks once the grant ends. The result is a maintenance burden that outstrips staff capacity and makes even the most ethically charged shimmer meaningless the moment the underlying asset decays or the framework breaks after a security update [Holmes et al. 2023]. To keep the pidgin realistic, any grammar of interfaces must be accompanied byneeds an underlayunderlying lexicon that names the conditions for preservation. Making the terms of maintenance explicit in early scoping meetings would let collaborators weigh visual ambition against long-term resilience, ensuring that folds and shimmers are backed by infrastructures capable of keeping them alive.

Data-capture politics. In this paper, I consider collections as given, yet many digital archives originate in contexts of injustice ranging from colonial extraction to surveillance regimes [Bonde Thylstrup 2019]. The principle of partiality — , with its license to blur, hide, or withhold — , mitigates some downstream harm, but it cannot undo the coercive conditions under which some of these records were first ‘captured.’ To confront that history the lexicon itself needs new terms. A consent ledger could travel with a record, logging who authorized what use and when that consent expires; a. A refusal register would document requests by source communities to suppress, restrict, or repatriate items; a sovereignty tag might mark materials governed by Indigenous data protocols such as CARE [Russo Carroll et al. 2020]. Embedding such terms — and, along with the accompanying technical affordances — specifications, would shiftextend the pidgin from merely styling access to actively reckoning with the structural violence that precedes visualization and would create pathwaysdesign for encounter to the conditions of capture, and open a path to restitution or deletion whenwhere justice demands it. However, what constitutes justice or violence depends on the specific situation. The same act may be perceived as preservation in one community and as a violation in another. Navigating these tensions requires a language that enables dialogue across value systems shaped by time and place without dissolving their differences.

Risk of oversimplification. Any pidgin gains its usefulness by limiting language to negotiable chunks. Rendering wanderer, fold, and shimmer as design heuristics inevitably compresses the dense strata of philosophies from which they spring. What begins as a mobile metaphor can become a decorative trope — “, an instruction to add a shimmer effect here” and “insert a fold there” — , detached from the histories the terms were meant to foreground. I therefore stress that the The pidgin’s brevity is a provisional bridge, not a destination. Each term should act as a prompt to return to its source traditions, to cite them, and to involve their living communities where possible. Put differently: the The pidgin itself must remain seamful [Hengesbach 2022]. Its]: its visible stitches should remind designers that behind every concise phrase lies a thicker fabric of theory and practice that must be revisited if the critical force of the concepts is not to fray.

Ocular-centrism. This project assumes that knowledge is encountered first and foremost through the eye: a wanderer glances across a visual field, folds reshape a graphic surface, and shimmer flashes as transient light. Such emphasis risks marginalizing archivescollections whose primary materials are sonic, haptic, or olfactoryhaptic, and it under-serves communities that approach collections through touch, voice, or vibration. Extending the pidgin therefore means recruiting new parts of speech. A term like echo‘echo’ might designate a reverberant relation that emerges only when sounds overlap in time; grain. Similarly, ‘grain’ could name the tactile residue that lingers after a page is handled; after-scent might capture olfactory traces that summon absent landscapes.. Developing such multisensory lexemes — terms, and pairing them with interface techniques that privilege hearing, or touch, or smell — would counter the bias toward sight and offer more inclusive grammars for archivescollections whose stories should resonate beyond the visual.

By briefly mentioning these limitations, I wish to acknowledge where the pidgin invites expansion. The gaps signal where new speakers can coin new terms that address technical plumbing, extraction histories, or cross-modal experiences. Treating incompleteness as a feature rather than a flaw keeps the language capable of absorbing critique.

Distance from archival practice. Admittedly, the conversation described here barely touches the daily work of description, delivery, and discovery. The people who write finding aids and answer reference queries are rarely involved when a collection interface is designed, and their perspectives may differ from the ones assumed above. Slowness, there, is not an ethic but a service failure. A term is only useful for a practitioner if it links to something already in their frame of reference. Fold fits in readily, since a finding aid is itself a folded structure, and most discovery interfaces render it badly. Wanderer fits since it suggests a kind of browsing that reference statistics have never recorded and failed to support. Shimmer attaches to nothing I can identify at this point. If this pidgin philosophy is to travel, the intention is not to simply propagate three words but to learn how they resonate with, and rub against, archival practices.

Asymmetry in the metaphor. A pidgin is not a meeting of equals. Its lexicon comes primarily from one of the languages in contact, while its grammar comes primarily from none of them [Thomason and Kaufman 1988]. Something is always supplying the words, and it is rarely the party with the least power, even if the direction of dominance is not uniform. Likewise, the settings described in this paper are not level either. Design and software vocabulary tends to set the terms, since it is attached to what will actually get built, while archivists and humanities scholars more often do the translating. This paper is not exempt, since some of the terms are in part borrowed from Indigenous thought, from communities who were not included when the borrowing happened. Naming a lexicon is itself an act of authority, and a pidgin philosophy that only celebrates hybridity would miss this. The more demanding question is not what the words mean but who gets to coin them, and whether the people who hold the material can shape a prototype as forcefully as the people who build it.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In thisThis paper I have attemptedset out to makedo three interwoven contributions. First, things. The first was to trace the emergence of a pidgin philosophy in the trading zone of archival studies, interface design, and the digital humanities, and to argue for data visualization documents vocabulary work as a hybrid language spoken among archivists, designers, and humanists. Second, a lexicon plantsmethodological stance. The second was to describe three seeds — terms, wanderer, fold, and shimmer — tracing, through their genealogieslineages, theoretical commitments, and practical usages. Third, a uses. The third was to synthesize them into a grammar binds those seeds into cross-cutting: the principles, a compact of relationality, temporality, and partiality, a phrase book for design dialoguecombining the terms, and a mixed-methodtripartite research framework for archival studies, digital humanities, interface design, and data visualization.

I opened with a workshop that was never meant to produce an interface. The aim was to stimulate a mixed group’s imagination about what a photo archive might become on screen, and to test a format for prompting that kind of conversation [Chen et al. 2014]. What the afternoon produced was a group who could, for a few hours, discuss the same collection in the same words. That idiom did not outlive the day, and no single interface can be traced to it. What travelled was the format: collaging proved a durable way of bringing people with different expertise into a common language, and it carried into more than a decade of visualization projects in Potsdam [Dörk et al. 2020]. The conversation itself likely informed Amber’s later redevelopment of its own website, and echoes of it persist in the terms gathered here. The afterlife was largely methodological. That is what this paper has been trying to name.

The lexicon and its grammar showsuggest how vocabulary work canmight function as a methodological resource for design and research method. Considering visitors as wanderers elevates the importance of foregrounds surprise and slowness and thus legitimizesmakes room for lingering in archive interfaces; modelling. Modeling interaction as folding operations keeps continuity and tension as desirable qualities of digital interfaces; lettingworth designing for. Letting shimmer appear and recede directs attention to the vitality and vulnerability of cultural collections and to the care required to maintain them. Eventhey require. Whether these few terms, combined through do such work beyond the phrase book, generate a range of design statements, whilesettings in which I have used them remains an open question, and the mixed-methodresearch framework offers asketches one way to study how those statements can hold up in practiceof finding out.

Yet anyAny pidgin remains provisional. Languages stay A contact language stays alive only by being spoken, revised, and sometimes contested; otherwise they turn into jargon and lose their power to move worlds.. The lexicon presented here is therefore meant as an opening, not rather than a closure. Future collaborations will doubtless need new terms that speak, for example, to sound archives or haptic collections and will uncover contexts in which the proposed termsthese three fail to evoke interest or imagination. As new situations arise, freshFresh words can be coined, old ones retired, and familiar phrases bentadjusted to better fit local ethics and aesthetics. Which words those turn out to be, and who gets to propose them, will be settled in the collaborations themselves rather than in a paper.
